After the rotor has moved due to the activated coil, the stator and rotor magnetic fields are in alignment.
Once the rotor aligns to the magnetic field of a single stator field, further energization of that same field coil will have no effect on the rotor.
To cause continuous or incremental rotation of the rotor, the stator fields must be sequentially activated from A through D.
Each activated coil corresponds to one quarter distance between rotor nodes.
If the sequence of coil activation (A-D) is maintained, rotor motion will continue.
To accomplish clockwise rotation, sequential activation of coils A, B, C, D is required.

To accomplish counter clockwise rotation, sequential activation of coils A, D, C, B is required.

Since there are 4 steps per stator cycle, 16 pulses are required for 1 complete revolution.
The most important part of Stepper Motor action is the sequence in which the coils are activated.
If a stator cycle is not completed, motor action will cease until pulses are resumed at the same place they ended.
As an example, suppose 5 pulses are sent to the Stepper for CW rotation in the sequence A, B, C, D, A.
The next sequence of pulses needed to continue rotation would be B, C, D, A, B.
If a step was missed in the sequence, motor action would not continue until the sequence was resumed, starting at the pulse that was missed or the pulse that corresponds to CCW rotation.
Assume B, D, A, B, C, was received rather than B, C, D, A, B.
At B the rotor would continue its CW rotation..............
At the next pulse, D, no rotor action would occur since pulse C was missed.
At the next pulse, A, CCW rotation would occur since the last correctly received pulse was B.
At the next pulse, B, CW rotation begins since the previous pulse was A.
The final pulse C continues the original CW rotation.
As you can see, two steps were missed by the pulses........

The stator pulse patterns discussed this far are called one phase energized since only one coil is activated at any instant of time.
One phase step patterns cause the the Stepper Motor to jerk due to time delays between pulses.
One phase step patterns are used when a minimum of current is required from the power supply.
TTRTRRTT
When smooth motor operation is required, two phase energized step patterns are employed.
In two phase step patterns, the next energized coil is turned on during the current step pulse.
In two phase step patterns, there is no time delay between pulses, resulting in jerk free operation.
In two phase step patterns, the power supply must generate more current since two pulses are used in one time period.
TTRTRRTT
Both the one phase and two phase step patterns are defined as full step patterns where each energized coil corresponds to one full step.
Another type of step pattern is called a half step pattern.
In a half step pattern, 2 coils must be energized to establish one complete step.
If only coil A is energized, rotor distance is 1/2 the distance traveled than if coils A and B were energized.
In a Stepper Motor with 50 rotor nodes and 4 stator windings, each half step causes 0.9 of rotor rotation.
PPR for the half step is 400. 100 stator cycles are required for one complete revolution of the rotor.
As you may have guessed, all values are twice that of a full step pattern.
